method: After freezing the decision and canonical record, returned to the downloaded 2026–2027 programme regulations and the current official thesis and preparation entries. Rebuilt the major credit breakdown and checked entry progression. Separately reconsidered the current UCR workbook’s literary content, course placements and the differences among plans against the final record. This is a separate same-AI pass.
findings: The target is the full-time Dutch registration. The OER also describes a separate English track in the same degree. The Dutch-track example is 180 EC: a 120 EC major and 60 EC profiling space. Article 3.5 and Appendices 1 and 2 give 75 EC of mandatory coursework, comprising the two foundational packages, Literary Toolbox and The Republic of Letters. The thesis is a separate 7.5 EC. Add one 30 EC depth package and one 7.5 EC context elective to reach 120 EC. Literature Across Borders and Retorica are the first-listed choices and independent of UCR fit. The five advanced courses in the four-course depth package and Literary Toolbox plus Current Debates, Republic of Letters and the thesis give 60 EC at level 3, above the 45 EC major minimum. The 60 EC profiling space must include a coherent 30 EC package, such as a minor, study abroad or another depth package. Choices requiring approval remain open.

The first year uses the two four-course foundational packages. The four depth courses run in order across the four blocks of Year 2, with Literary Toolbox in Block 3. Retorica is in Block 4 and may be placed in Year 3 if it conflicts with the depth course. The Year 3 Republic of Letters course is in Block 1. The thesis requires at least 120 EC and 22.5 EC at level 3, both reached on the standard progression after completing the first two years including profiling and the depth package. The thesis can follow Republic of Letters in a later block. The graduation requirements separately include at least 45 advanced EC in the major.

All three options have direct literary study. The conflict plan now includes a stronger literary spine and retains substantive historical and social context. The other two plans retain their course selections. The comparison distinguishes direct literary content from related art, media and social-science context and from the required thesis.
